articleTitle: Furfural and ageing: how are they related
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Insulating Liquids (Ref. No. 1999/119)
abstract: Cellulose degradation is a complex process which is accelerated by the combined effect of temperature, water and oxygen, all of them available to the cellulose in the environment of the transformer. Several mechanisms for the thermal degradation of cellulose have been proposed, depending on whether the predominant step is pyrolysis or hydrolysis of the glucose units. In the first case, pyrolysis of glucose, the reaction proceeds via levoglucosan (1,6-anhydro-P-D-glucopyranose) a dehydrated sugar which, after a series of bond rearrangements and further losses of water and formaldehyde (or hydrogen plus carbon monoxide) yield furfuraldehyde among other products. The hydrolysis of glucose units proceeds through the formation of an epoxide or an enol followed by internal rearrangements and further dehydration and elimination of formaldehyde to yield furfuraldehyde and other products. The connection between the deterioration in the material properties and the formation of ageing products is the degree of polymerisation, the number of anhydroglucose units in the cellulose chain. The degree of polymerisation proves to be the most informative parameter for assessing the ageing or the progress of ageing of cellulose.

articleTitle: New insulating fluids for transformers based on biodegradable high oleic vegetable oil and ester fluid
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Insulating Liquids (Ref. No. 1999/119)
abstract: The development of new insulating materials is guided by multiple parameters, as new environmental requirements and other safety or economical considerations. Therefore the transformer manufacturers have to face new specifications linked with these requirements. As these requirements are different from country to country, we can expect different approaches for the different markets. ISO and IEC have issued guides to consider these aspects. As ester or vegetable fluids are more expensive in comparison with mineral oil, it is important to optimize the design of the windings in order to take all the benefits of such modern fluids, beside the fire behavior and the other environmental aspects (toxicity, water pollution, waste treatment, etc). The use of ester fluids is common now, and much experience has been accumulated during the last decade. The vegetable oil is a new candidate to replace mineral oils in the future. Therefore this report is mostly dedicated to this new technology which represents a promising market. The development of a biodegradable electrical insulating fluid from high oleic vegetable oil sources is described. This type of oil was selected due to the inherent higher stability of high oleic oils over commercial grade oils. However, the selected oil had to be further purified to improve electrical properties, and special additives were used to enhance the oxidative stability in the environment of electrical equipment. The electrical equipment specifically targeted for immediate use was distribution transformers.

articleTitle: Insulating oil in service: is it fit for purpose?
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Insulating Liquids (Ref. No. 1999/119)
abstract: Insulating oil is designed to dissipate heat, and act as a coolant and electrical insulator in power transformers. During operation it is subjected to heat and materials that are not compatible with the oil. Provided the insulating oil has been supplied to the agreed specification, it is the user's responsibility to make sure that the oil is in good condition and fit for purpose. In order to evaluate the oil condition, oil samples should be taken from the equipment and tested. Details of the oil sampling technique are outlined in IEC 60475 (6). Frequency of oil sampling and testing is given in IEC 60422. Oil testing and classification of oil in service are briefly discussed.

articleTitle: Data mining applied to transformer oil analysis data
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Insulating Liquids (Ref. No. 1999/119)
abstract: Analysis of oil samples is a standard technique in the electricity industry for monitoring the condition of oil filled plant. Samples are typically taken annually, with more frequent sampling where there is a possible problem. Analyses performed on the oil include: dissolved gas analysis (DGA); colour; moisture level; acidity; breakdown voltage; and Furfuraldehyde (FFA) content. In DGA, the gases usually considered are: hydrogen; methane (CH/sub 4/); ethane (C/sub 2/H/sub 6/); ethylene (C/sub 2/H/sub 4/); acetylene (C/sub 2/H/sub 2/); carbon monoxide; and carbon dioxide. Variations in the levels of individual gases, or ratios of particular gases, may indicate a problem with the plant. This situation is complicated by the fact that the levels of dissolved gas measured can be affected by the sampling technique and conditions, the laboratory performing the analysis and the duration of sample storage prior to analysis. The results of oil analysis undertaken by The UK National Grid Company are recorded in a database as records of gas concentrations (in ppm). These records are currently analysed by conventional methods; the reported exercise used unsupervised neural networks to unearth further information.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Insulating Liquids (Ref. No. 1999/119)
abstract: Electrotechnical fluids are handled through the BSI Electrical Department, of which there are four major segments. The particular segment involved for electrical oil is the General Electrical Engineering segment, and the specific committee in that segment is GEL/10. GEL/10 is responsible for some 44 standards encompassing both liquids, gases and the associated testing procedures. The relevant standards of concern are BS 148/98 and IEC 296/82. These two standards are very similar but the author highlights the major differences between the specifications. Other major standards are briefly mentioned.

articleTitle: The role of oil analysis in the ESI
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Insulating Liquids (Ref. No. 1999/119)
abstract: The author takes a broad overview of the chemistry of materials and analytical techniques used in the laboratory. Techniques employed by the analytical chemist have contributed to the knowledge and understanding. This has enabled sound engineering decisions on the management of electrical plant to be made, whilst at the same time assisting planning for replacement and design of new equipment. A short overview of some chemistry on oils and their properties is given followed by some common techniques employed in the laboratory for assessment of the plant and other dielectrics. A few notes are given on the possible areas for future analysis and how the environmental and consumer pressures may change the emphasis on analysis in the future.

articleTitle: Synthetic aromatic liquids for the electrical industry
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Insulating Liquids (Ref. No. 1999/119)
abstract: Several categories of synthetic liquids are used in the electrical industry: including aromatic hydrocarbons which are mainly used in capacitors and cables. Elf Atochem has specialised in the manufacturing of aromatic hydrocarbons which are briefly outlined. The properties of the aromatic liquids including composition, dielectric properties, thermal stability, breakdown strength, ageing properties on wound models, and toxicological, environmental and fire properties.

articleTitle: Oil in 11 kV switchgear. Service performance
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Insulating Liquids (Ref. No. 1999/119)
abstract: There has been much interest in the adoption of condition based maintenance regimes. One area which has attracted particular interest is the maintenance of 11 kV oil filled switchgear. Electricity companies have undertaken considerable work assessing the availability and effectiveness of techniques to assess the condition of switchgear noninvasively. A number of companies have also completed detailed reliability centred maintenance (RCM) studies in order to identify the critical factors which affect the safe and efficient operation of this equipment. EA Technology on behalf of many of the RECs have undertaken both joint investigations of the condition of 11 kV switchgear and many individual investigations of switchgear failures. Combining the results of these various studies it has become clear that in general the condition of oil filled switchgear in service is very good and that the critical factor in determining the degradation of components within switchgear and therefore ensuring satisfactory and safe long term performance is the condition of the oil. In order to move towards condition based maintenance, information on the condition of the oil is therefore seen as paramount. As a result of this, EA Technology has carried out an assessment of the condition of oil in service and used this to consider critically the processes of oil degradation. The appreciation of these factors has enabled significant progress to be made towards a condition based maintenance strategy. This paper briefly summarises the outcome of this work and illustrates the benefits and opportunities that have resulted.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Insulating Liquids (Ref. No. 1999/119)
abstract: Bioremediation is the process whereby naturally occurring micro-organisms are used to digest chemicals into harmless products such as carbon dioxide, water and microbial biomass. A wide range of chemicals can be degraded in this way including oils and greases. However, the time scales over which this degradation can occur can vary enormously due to limitations imposed by various factors. These factors include numbers of organisms present, nutrient levels, heat, moisture, oxygen levels within the soil and the complexity of the contaminant that needs to be degraded. For example, linear compounds are more easily degraded than ring compounds. Soils generally contain around 10/sup 6/ micro-organisms per gram, but this needs to be boosted to a level of 10/sup 8/ per gram ideally by natural multiplication over a period of time. The increase can be achieved through the addition of selected microbes, however, their rate of increase in population is not always as high as that of the indigenous microbe population. The microorganisms are most effective under particular conditions, for example in the presence of nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorous and at temperatures of 20-25/spl deg/C. Bioremediation can be carried out in two ways, ex-situ and in-situ.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Insulating Liquids (Ref. No. 1999/119)
abstract: Mineral oils have been used as insulating liquids for more than 100 years starting in a transformer application. Today's mineral oil products are of course very different from the original product but the sources are still the same and partly the refining methods. The availability is good and compared with synthetic and other products life cycle analysis are very positive. What have changed are the requirements and the refining techniques to achieve desired properties. These refining techniques are described as is the oil chemistry.

articleTitle: Oil disposal: options and legal requirements. A short overview
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Insulating Liquids (Ref. No. 1999/119)
abstract: The normal processes used to manage oil involve its maintenance. The maintenance processes used, including filtration and regeneration, are being looked at by the UK Environment Agency as activities that potentially could need a waste management licence or an exemption from waste management licensing. Here, the author presents a short overview of the options and legal requirements for waste oil disposal.
